Chapter 9: The Brain’s Blind Spots—Denial, Confabulation, and the Limits of Self-Knowledge.
Have you ever caught yourself ignoring something obvious, just because it was too hard to face? We all do it from time to time. For some folks though, this denial goes much deeper—it becomes a kind of shield, protecting the mind from truths that just feel too heavy to carry.
Picture this: after a stroke, a woman can’t move one side of her body. Yet, when asked, she claims she can move her arm just fine. She even tries to lift it, fails, and then simply shrugs—saying, “I just don’t feel like moving it right now.” Her family is confused, but the doctors, they’ve seen this before. The mind, unable to accept what’s happened, actually invents a story to keep the sense of being whole.
Or take another example—a man struggling with memory loss. He starts greeting total strangers like old friends, and whenever he can’t remember something, he weaves together detailed tales to fill the gaps. The thing is, he’s not lying on purpose. These confabulations are just his brain’s way of making sense of a world that’s suddenly full of holes. It’s almost as if the mind would rather have a story—any story—than face a blank.
What’s really fascinating is, most of us don’t even notice our own blind spots. Our brains are experts at hiding their own mistakes, smoothing over contradictions, and keeping our personal stories neat and tidy. And honestly, that’s not a bug—it’s a feature. It’s how we keep going, even when things don’t quite add up.
This all leads to a pretty humbling realization: no matter how hard we try, self-knowledge is always going to have its limits. These blind spots aren’t just the result of illness or injury—they’re an everyday part of being human. We all tweak our memories, explain away our choices, and quietly ignore those facts that don’t quite fit.
Our brain’s ability to deny or confabulate can protect us, sure—but sometimes, it can send us down the wrong path.
So, what’s the takeaway here? These stories remind us to approach our own minds with a little humility. To accept that there will always be things we can’t see or know, and to stay open to the idea that we might be wrong—even about ourselves.
